system.summary: The main system: one- and two-digit codes with no spaces; a and o each have two codes; code 74 is che; code 36 is read as a null. The earlier system (R4034 to R4038) uses the archive's key table R4033, with letter codes and word signs.
system.notes: distinct_symbols counts the code types of key/key-main.tsv (the main system). The nomenclator has 69 entries: code 74 (che) of the main key, and the 68 word signs of the archive's table (names, titles and common words). Diacritics: a bar over the digits marks a word sign of the earlier system; the main system has none.

prior_solution.where: No earlier decipherment of these letters is known to me. The archive's key table R4033 is a key of the earlier system, not a decipherment. Ferrai (1882), p. 136, note 1, prints the wording of a sister letter of R4054, not R4054.

Read as sentences: R4035, R4037 and R4038 build coherent Italian (reading review grade B, read in part: 26 of 29, 201 of 243 and 41 of 50 cipher words sure); R4034 does so only in passages 4, 6 and 8 and R4036 does not, and both stay decoded, not read. texts.label: R4034, Cosimo I to Niccolini, 17 December 1537
texts.summary: My words, a paraphrase of the reading: The tithes. Cosimo writes that he begged someone not to burden a party, at present so exhausted, with such a levy; the code for that party has no value. His Majesty's aid is named. A doubtful word sign that the table gives as the Emperor stands at four places: his favour, his mind, his coming near Italy. After "il prefat", a doubtful barred sign gives the table's King of France; cut otherwise, it gives "Arciuescouo" (archbishop). Niccolini is to draw the matter out as long as he can, with no offer, because time can bring much advantage. The passage probably names the case of "Altopaso" (perhaps Altopascio).
texts.note: Reading in sentences and English translation on the record page, made from the decode. Counts by the word rule (an estimate): 112 cipher words, 77 sure, 35 holes; read share 0.688. Under the read bar; 0 of 8 sentences and fragments have at most one hole in ten words. README.md. Integration review of PR #822 (20 Nov 2026, AI agent): stays decoded, not read; it builds sentences only in passages 4, 6 and 8, and the clear words around its short cipher runs are not in the folder.

texts.label: R4035, Cosimo I to Niccolini, 24 December 1537
texts.summary: My words, a paraphrase of the reading: The passage names those who have grown and fattened on the ruin of others and on ours, and His Holiness doing worse to this city and state. It ends: "to proceed in this business as the Prince will do at Genoa".
texts.note: Reading in sentences and English translation on the record page, made from the decode. Counts by the word rule (an estimate): 29 cipher words, 26 sure, 3 holes; read share 0.897. If code 29 = t, from ciphertext, does not count as given by the key: 17 sure, 12 holes (0.586). Under the read bar; 1 of 2 sentences and fragments have at most one hole in ten words. README.md. Integration review of PR #822 (20 Nov 2026, AI agent): read in part, grade B; 3 holes, one over the floor for a text under 40 cipher words. A word on code 29 counts as given by the key (NOTES.md).

texts.label: R4037, Cosimo I to Niccolini, 16 February 1538
texts.summary: My words, a paraphrase of the reading: The two papal tithes on Florence. Cosimo writes that he was given to understand that he should proceed in this business as he sees "the prince … Doria" and the city of Genoa proceed. A proposal: to be content with half of the two tithes, one raised now and one a year later, by a Florentine commissioner whom His Holiness appoints. Church censures and an interdict are named.
texts.note: Reading in sentences and English translation on the record page, made from the decode. Counts by the word rule (an estimate): 243 cipher words, 201 sure, 42 holes; read share 0.827. If code 29 = t, from ciphertext, does not count as given by the key: 159 sure, 84 holes (0.654). Under the read bar; 1 of 7 sentences and fragments have at most one hole in ten words. README.md. The five numbered Italian passages on r4037.md (seven sentences) read as sentences against their English: all are coherent Italian (Cosimo was given to understand, at a court named by an unread sign, that he should proceed in the business of the tithes as Prince Doria and the city of Genoa do; they have reached no agreement; half of the two tithes, one now and one in a year, through a Florentine commissioner deputed by His Holiness; censures and interdict would be borne with patience). B: raw. texts.label: R4038, Cosimo I to Niccolini, 4 March 1538
texts.summary: My words, a paraphrase of the reading: Niccolini is to accept the extension "se[c]ondo Clemente" (perhaps "as under Pope Clement"), as they have said, and have it issued as in the copy that is sent to him. If they knew of it, they would not want it so broad, or would want better terms. Any further advantage is left to him.

texts.label: R4039, Cosimo I to Niccolini, 4 October 1538
texts.summary: Cosimo writes about a marriage alliance and "the matter of the wife". His intention in the matter of the wife has always been the same, from the start until now. He encloses a copy of a letter. Its aim is to cut off this negotiation entirely, because it is too contrary to his mind. He warns Niccolini about one man. That man is not to be trusted, and he fears to lose "his penitentiary" (an office). The same man acted against Duke Alessandro "of good memory", and against Cosimo at his arrival.

texts.label: R4047, Cosimo I to Niccolini, 18 January 1539
texts.summary: Cosimo writes about a "motu proprio" (an act that the pope issues on his own initiative) and about how to use it. The matter "would turn to our great advantage, more than theirs". He hopes that they will do it, and he says that it is right to act "at the right time and place". He wants to make them feel "a great suspicion". When "this fear" is taken away, "another suspicion" stays "in this cause".

texts.label: R4054, Cosimo I to Niccolini, 11 August 1539
texts.summary: Cosimo writes about the arrest of one Biagio della Campana. The passage also names Giulio, the natural son of Duke Alessandro. Biagio della Campana had always kept company with "the sons of Bartolomeo Valori". He was taken two years before and examined. Many crimes were found in him, which deserved every punishment. A sentence of the Balìa condemned him, and he was sent to the fortress of Pisa. Later he was freed, with many other prisoners.
